A.explanation: The area is $\frac{1}{2}Fx$ only for a straight-line force-extension graph obeying Hooke's law. If the graph curves, the area is not a triangle.

B.explanation: Stored elastic potential energy equals the area only if stretching is elastic. Beyond the elastic limit some work becomes heat and permanent deformation, not stored energy.

C.explanation: For a varying force, small work $F\Delta x$ summed over the extension is the area under the $F$-$x$ graph, so the area always equals work done in stretching.

D.explanation: Area depends on length, cross-sectional area and maximum force and extension, so different sized wires of the same material give different areas.

hints: Notice the axes are force $F$ against extension $x$, and the question says increasing values of $F$ with no promise that the graph is a straight line.
Recall that work done by a varying force is the sum of $F \Delta x$ strips, which is the area under an $F$-$x$ graph with unit $\text{N m} = \text{J}$.
Ask whether all that work must stay as $\frac{1}{2}Fx$ or as recoverable elastic energy if the wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit.
walkthrough: Identify what is plotted: $F$ on the vertical axis and $x$ on the horizontal axis for a wire stretched to larger and larger $F$.
State the governing rule: work done in a small stretch is $\Delta W = F \Delta x$, so total work $W = \text{sum of } F\Delta x$ strips.
Explain the graph link: the sum of rectangular strips $F\Delta x$ is the area under the force-extension curve, with units $\text{N} \times \text{m} = \text{J}$.
Distinguish the special cases: $\frac{1}{2}Fx$ is the triangular area only when $F$ is proportional to $x$, and elastic potential energy equals the work only when no plastic deformation occurs.
Conclude that the area must always represent the energy transferred in by the stretching force, which is the work done. This is option C.
